title: Frontier Technology in Frontier Markets? Financing Global AI
text:
### Frontier Technology in Frontier Markets? Financing Global AI Entrepreneurship∗

Gilles Q. Hacheme AI4Innov

Ebehi Iyoha Harvard Business School

Abdoulaye Ndiaye NYU Stern School of Business

Noureini S. Souleymane AI4Innov

November 2026

Abstract Does the global diffusion of artificial intelligence (AI) extend to the creation and financing of the firms that build it? Using a novel dataset of 116,795 startups founded between 2015 and 2022 across 172 countries, we link company descriptions and financing histories to the employment and education records of founders, early employees, and potential investors. We document a stark divergence between the real and financial sides of global AI entrepreneurship. On the real side, AI startups everywhere display the hallmarks of a general-purpose technology: in every world region, they target more customer sectors than comparable non-AI startups and are more likely to sell horizontal products that apply across industries. Moreover, following the release of ChatGPT, startups whose baseline tasks were more amenable to AI expanded the breadth of their work activities and commercial staffing. Yet the financing advantage that such scalable businesses command is sharply localized. AI startups raise 151 percent more annual capital than non-AI peers in North America and 181 percent more in the Middle East, compared with 42 percent more in East Asia, 16 percent more in Europe, and no detectable premium in Africa, Latin America, or South Asia. Accounting for targeted customer markets, founder credentials, early-team human capital, and local investor characteristics explains part of the gap in Latin America but leaves the broader global divide intact. In Africa, half of all AI funding goes to basic compute and data-center infrastructure; excluding these providers reveals that African AI product startups raise 57 percent less than non-AI peers. These patterns provide an early warning that AI may reach users around the world without building firms around the world.

#### 1 Introduction

Will artificial intelligence narrow or widen the income gap between rich and poor countries? 
The history of earlier general-purpose technologies gives reason for concern. Over the past 
two centuries, the lags with which developing countries adopted new technologies shrank, but 
the intensity with which they used those technologies, and their incomes, diverged (Comin 
and Hobijn, 2010; Comin and Mestieri, 2018). Theoretical models warn that AI could follow a 
similar or even more polarizing path: when a new technology substitutes for labor or requires 
deep stocks of complementary capital, advanced economies capture the lion’s share of the 
gains while developing economies risk losing their comparative advantage in tradable tasks 
(Korinek and Stiglitz, 2021; Alonso et al., 2022; Cazzaniga et al., 2024). 
Because the aggregate productivity effects of AI will take years to materialize in national 
accounts, economists have turned to early warning indicators such as occupational employment 
shifts in the United States (Brynjolfsson et al., 2025a) and cross-country disparities in the 
usage of large language models (Appel et al., 2025; Sajadieh et al., 2026). Yet usage statistics 
capture only the consumption of AI tools built elsewhere. For developing and emerging 
economies to capture the rents, high-skill employment, and spillovers of technological change, 
they must also build and scale firms that produce AI and adapt it to local markets (Kalyani 
et al., 2025). Because venture financing and entry decisions are inherently forward-looking, 
the capital markets that back new ventures offer an early, high-stakes signal of where the 
supply side of the global AI economy is taking root (Bena et al., 2026). 
This paper studies the global geography of AI entrepreneurship through the lens of startup 
financing. We define AI firms as startups that develop or sell AI products at any layer of the 
supply chain (applications, models, data tools, infrastructure, or compute) rather than firms 
whose employees merely use AI internally. Comparing AI and non-AI startups within the 
same country, founding cohort, and funding year, we ask four questions. First, do AI startups 
around the world build broader, more scalable businesses than non-AI startups, both in the 
customer markets they target and in how they organize work? Second, do capital markets 
reward this breadth with an “AI financing premium,” and is that premium uniform across 
world regions? Third, where the financing premium is absent, can the gap be explained by 
differences in customer demand, the human capital of founders and early employees, or the 
characteristics and networks of local investors? Finally, what do the remaining gaps imply 
for the complementary infrastructure and institutions required to spread the gains from AI? 
To answer these questions, we assemble a global dataset covering 116,795 startups founded 
between 2015 and 2022 across 172 countries in seven world regions: North America, Europe 
and Central Asia, East Asia and the Pacific, Latin America and the Caribbean, the Middle 

East, South Asia, and Africa. We combine comprehensive company and deal records from 
PitchBook with data from Stears to ensure deep coverage of African ventures, including 
startups that never raised external capital or subsequently closed. We link these firms to 
the employment and educational histories of 52,203 founders and 719,358 early nonfounder 
employees from Revelio Labs, and to investor and fund-commitment records from Preqin. 
Using a large language model to apply a standardized questionnaire to company descriptions 
and archived web pages, we identify 42,312 AI producers and map each startup’s targeted 
customers across 99 three-digit NAICS industries and 20 broad sectors. We further link 
employee occupations to O*NET work activities and task-level ratings of LLM exposure 
(Eloundou et al., 2024) to track how startups organize their workforces over time. 
Our first set of results establishes that, on the real side of the firm, AI startups everywhere 
exhibit the defining traits of a general-purpose technology (GPT) (Bresnahan and Trajtenberg, 
1995). Across all seven regions, AI startups target significantly broader customer markets than 
non-AI startups founded in the same country and year—serving 0.102 more broad sectors on 
average and proving 16 to 23 percentage points more likely to offer horizontal products that 
apply across industries. These differences are not artifacts of how firms market themselves; 
they hold conditional on data source and description length, and they are already visible in 
archived business descriptions written near founding. Furthermore, when AI startups target 
multiple industries, they do not string together unrelated markets: holding ordinary task 
overlap fixed, the industries targeted by multi-sector AI firms share tasks with significantly 
higher suitability for AI (0.080 higher on a zero-to-one scale). AI thus enables startups in 
every region to build a single technological capability and redeploy it across diverse customer 
sectors. 
This product breadth is mirrored by organizational expansion inside the firm. Realizing the 
returns to a GPT requires complementary adjustments in how work is organized (Brynjolfsson 
et al., 2021). Using a quarterly panel of roughly 63,000 startups from 2021 through 2025, 
we examine how firms adjusted their workforces around the public release of ChatGPT in 
November 2022. To avoid endogenous post-release adjustments, we measure each firm’s 
baseline task amenability to AI in December 2021 as the AI-weighted overlap between its 
workforce’s tasks and the average industry’s task profile. Controlling for firm fixed effects, 
country-by-quarter shocks, and baseline firm task suitability, we show that startups with 
higher baseline task amenability evolved in parallel with less-amenable peers prior to late 
2022, but diverged sharply afterward. Following ChatGPT’s release, a one-standard-deviation 
higher baseline amenability is associated with 1.09 additional distinct work activities on 
average in 2023–2025 (rising to 1.54 by late 2025) and a 1.62 percentage point increase in the 
likelihood of employing commercial staff. Rather than merely displacing labor, generative 

AI appears to help startups broaden their internal scope and commercialize across wider 
markets (Acemoglu and Restrepo, 2019). 
If AI startups in every region build broader products, and if AI-amenable organizations 
expand their operational and commercial reach, standard theories of innovation finance 
predict that AI startups should command a financing premium over comparable non-AI 
startups (Babina et al., 2024; Hoberg and Phillips, 2025; Kim and Koning, 2026). Our second 
set of results shows that while an AI financing premium exists on average (AI startups raise 
87 percent more annual funding than non-AI peers) its geography is highly unequal. We 
estimate annual funding between 2019 and 2025 using Poisson pseudo-maximum likelihood 
(PPML) with country-by-funding-year, country-by-founding-year, and firm-age fixed effects. 
Because these fixed effects absorb the aggregate supply of venture capital, macroeconomic 
conditions, and financial development in each country and year, our estimates isolate how 
investors value AI startups relative to non-AI startups operating in the same local market. 
The regional divergence is striking. In North America and the Middle East, AI startups 
raise 151 percent and 181 percent more annual funding, respectively, than non-AI startups 
founded in the same country and year. In East Asia and the Pacific, the premium is 42 
percent; in Europe and Central Asia, it is just 16 percent. In Africa, Latin America and the 
Caribbean, and South Asia, the AI financing premium vanishes entirely. Relative to North 
America, the AI-to-non-AI funding ratio is 54 percent lower in Europe, 63 percent lower 
in South Asia, 65 percent lower in Africa, and 76 percent lower in Latin America. These 
patterns are robust to classifying AI status from archived website descriptions near founding, 
mitigating concerns that successfully funded startups simply rebrand as AI firms later in life. 
Why do investors give AI startups a large funding premium in North America while 
offering no premium at all in Africa, Latin America, and South Asia, despite AI startups 
building broader businesses in all of these regions? In the third part of the paper, we test 
three primary candidate explanations by sequentially introducing firm, worker, and investor 
controls on a consistent sample of 554,513 firm-years and tracking how each region’s funding 
gap relative to North America changes. 
First, we test a demand explanation: AI startups in developing regions might target 
customer industries with weaker global growth or lower willingness to pay for AI. Absorbing 
worldwide demand shocks via principal-customer-industry-by-year fixed effects and controlling
